cc.t: Referral.
Evaluation.
Waiting.
A phone that may never ring.
The American Society of Transplantation read a federal kidney plan, and said it welcomes it.
Welcomes.
Say that word to the person in the chair tonight.
Read the statement.
No number.
No deadline.
No funded commitment.
No seat for the patient.
In twenty twenty-four, one hundred forty-three thousand, nine hundred eighty-two adults were listed for a kidney.
About one in ten had waited five years or longer.
Four thousand, nine hundred and one were removed because they got too sick to transplant.
Three thousand, seven hundred forty-three died waiting.
Nearly five thousand people crossed off the list, and not one of them counted among the dead.
Then the waste.
In one year, nine thousand, six hundred eighty of thirty-two thousand kidneys were thrown away.
Twenty-nine point seven percent.
Families gave those organs on the worst day of their lives.
More than twenty-six million attempts to place them. Still discarded.
Where is the demand for perfusion?
For faster placement?
For accountability when centers turn organs down?
Who decides?
Fourteen board members.
Physicians. Surgeons. Scientists. One transplant nurse.
No patient. No care partner.
And nominations go only to people already sitting in their meetings.
Corporate partners meet with that board every year.
Patients get a caregiver toolkit, and a link to register as a donor.
In twenty twenty, the AST wrote that for-profit organizations inherently are incentivized to prolong dialysis over offering transplantation.
Six years.
Where is the fix?
The federal plan sets policy direction.
Direction costs nothing.
Direction has no deadline.
Seat patients and care partners on the board, with full votes.
Publish a dated target for cutting discards.
Fund real perfusion and preservation.
Report every year how many listed patients die, or are removed as too sick.
This is not leadership.
It is public relations.
And we have buried too many people to keep pretending otherwise.
